content: Cefotetan disodium is a second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic approved by the FDA for treating various infections, including urinary tract infections, lower respiratory tract infections, skin and skin structure infections, gynecologic infections, intra-abdominal infections, and bone and joint infections. It is also used for the prevention of postoperative infections. Common side effects include diarrhea and nausea. Indications and Dosage for Adults: 1. Urinary Tract Infections: Caused by organisms such as E. coli, Klebsiella spp., Proteus mirabilis, and others. Dosage: 500 mg every 12 hours IV; or 1-2 g every 24 hours IV; or 1-2 g every 12 hours IV. 2. Lower Respiratory Tract Infections: Caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus (penicillinase and non-penicillinase producing strains), Haemophilus influenzae (including ampicillin-resistant strains), and others. Dosage: 1-2 g every 12 hours IV for 5-10 days. Severe cases: 2 g every 12 hours IV for 5-10 days. Life-threatening cases: 3 g every 12 hours IV for 5-10 days. 3. Skin and Skin Structure Infections: Caused by Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Streptococcus pyogenes, and others. Dosage for mild to moderate cases: 2 g every 24 hours IV or 1 g every 12 hours IV for 5-10 days. Severe cases: 2 g every 12 hours IV for 5-10 days. 4. Gynecologic Infections: Caused by organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus agalactiae, E. coli, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and others. Dosage: 1-2 g every 12 hours IV for 5-10 days. Severe cases: 2 g every 12 hours IV for 5-10 days. Life-threatening cases: 3 g every 12 hours IV for 5-10 days. 5. Intra-abdominal Infections: Caused by E. coli, Klebsiella spp., Streptococcus spp., and others. Dosage: 1-2 g IV once, administered 30-60 minutes prior to surgery. Cefotetan does not have activity against Chlamydia trachomatis. When treating pelvic inflammatory disease where C. trachomatis is suspected, additional antichlamydial coverage is required. Pediatric Use: Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients have not been established. Contraindications: Patients with known allergies to cephalosporins. Patients with a history of cephalosporin-associated hemolytic anemia. Warnings: Before initiating therapy, assess for previous hypersensitivity reactions to cefotetan, cephalosporins, penicillins, or other drugs. Cross-reactivity between beta-lactam antibiotics is documented and may occur in up to 10% of penicillin-allergic patients. If an allergic reaction occurs, discontinue the drug immediately. Severe hypersensitivity reactions may require emergency treatment, including epinephrine, oxygen, IV fluids, antihistamines, corticosteroids, and airway management. Immune-mediated hemolytic anemia has been reported with cephalosporins, including cefotetan. Severe cases, including fatalities, have been documented. Monitor for signs of hemolytic anemia, and discontinue the drug if anemia develops. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported and may range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. If CDAD is suspected, discontinue unnecessary antibiotics and initiate appropriate treatment. Adverse Reactions: Common: Diarrhea, nausea, rash, and itching. Hematologic: Eosinophilia, positive Coombs test, thrombocytosis, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and prolonged prothrombin time. Hepatic: Elevated ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, and LDH. Renal: Rare reports of nephrotoxicity. Local: Phlebitis and discomfort at the injection site. Rare: Anaphylactic reactions, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and seizures (especially in patients with renal impairment). Drug Interactions: Concomitant use with aminoglycosides may potentiate nephrotoxicity; monitor renal function closely. May cause false-positive results for glucose in urine tests using certain methods (e.g., Clinitest®, Benedict's solution). Use enzymatic glucose oxidase-based tests instead. Use in Specific Populations: Pregnancy: Category B. Animal studies have shown no harm to the fetus, but adequate studies in pregnant women are lacking. Use only if clearly needed. Nursing Mothers: Excreted in low concentrations in human milk. Use with caution. Geriatric Use: No significant differences in safety or effectiveness observed, but elderly patients are more likely to have impaired renal function. Monitor renal function and adjust dosage as needed. Renal Impairment: Adjust dosage based on creatinine clearance. Pharmacology: Cefotetan exerts its bactericidal effect by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis. It is active against a wide range of aerobic and anaerobic gram-positive and gram-negative organisms. The methoxy group at the 7-alpha position provides stability against beta-lactamases. Approximately 88% of cefotetan is plasma protein-bound. It is primarily excreted unchanged by the kidneys, with high urinary concentrations achieved. Patient Counseling: Inform patients that diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and usually resolves after discontinuation. However, if watery or bloody stools occur, even weeks after completing therapy, contact a physician immediately. Advise patients to complete the full course of therapy as prescribed, even if they feel better early in treatment, to prevent bacterial resistance. Warn against alcohol consumption within 72 hours of cefotetan administration due to the risk of a disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, sweating, headache, tachycardia). Storage: Store at 20° to 25°C (68° to 77°F).
